# How to Use Copilot to Plan a Small Event or Project

By the end of this guide you'll have a ready-to-use plan with tasks, owners and dates for any small project or event — built with Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant that lives inside Word, Edge and Windows. This is for anyone who has ever opened a blank document and wondered, "Right… where do I even start?"

## Before you start
- A **Microsoft account** (the same one you use for Outlook, OneDrive or Hotmail). Sign up free at microsoft.com if you don't have one.
- Access to **Copilot** — you can use it free in the Edge browser (look for the Copilot icon in the top-right), at copilot.microsoft.com, or inside Microsoft 365 apps like Word. Some advanced features (like Copilot inside Word) need a paid Microsoft 365 subscription, but the web version is enough for this guide.
- A **rough idea** of what you're planning — even two sentences is fine.
- About **15–20 minutes** for your first run-through.

## Step 1 — Open Copilot and start a new chat
Open your web browser and go to **copilot.microsoft.com**, or open Microsoft Edge and look for the **Copilot** icon (a small colorful ribbon) in the top-right corner of the browser. What you see is a clean chat window with a text box at the bottom that says something like *"Ask me anything…"*. After you click or tap into the box, a blinking cursor appears — that's where you'll type. If your screen looks different (for example, Copilot might already be open in a side panel in Edge), any chat-style box that says "Ask Copilot" or "Message Copilot" works the same way. You'll know it worked when the text box is active and ready for you to type.

💬 Example: Type this to begin — *"Help me plan a small project."*

## Step 2 — Describe the event or project in plain words
Click into the chat box and write a short description of what you're planning. On screen you'll see your message appear in a chat bubble, and shortly after, Copilot will start typing a reply below it. What happens next is Copilot reads your description and, usually, asks a couple of clarifying questions (like how many people, what date, or what your budget looks like). If your Copilot opens as a side panel instead of a full page, look for the same text box at the bottom of the panel — the layout works the same. You'll know it worked when Copilot replies with either a draft plan or a few smart follow-up questions.

💬 Example: *"I want to organize a community bake sale on Saturday 14 March at our local hall. About 8 helpers, budget around $300. I need a simple plan with tasks, who does what, and deadlines."*

## Step 3 — Ask Copilot to break it into tasks and owners
Now reply in the chat and ask Copilot to turn the idea into a structured plan. What you'll see on screen is Copilot producing a numbered or bulleted list of tasks, each with a suggested owner and a suggested deadline. After the reply finishes, a small toolbar (icons like copy, regenerate, thumbs up/down) appears under the answer — that's your clue the response is complete. If instead of a list you get a short paragraph, just reply and ask for it as a table or a numbered list; Copilot will redo it. You'll know it worked when you can see a clear list of 8–15 tasks with names (or "TBD") and dates next to them.

💬 Example: *"Great, please turn that into a numbered task list with a suggested owner for each task and a deadline in the week before the event."*

## Step 4 — Refine the plan by asking follow-up questions
This is where Copilot really earns its keep. Look at the list it produced and pick the bits that don't quite fit — the date that's too tight, the task you forgot, the owner you want to swap. Type a follow-up into the same chat box, and Copilot will rewrite the relevant part of the plan in place. What you see after sending is a new version of the plan, with your change folded in. If your plan ever disappears off the screen, just scroll up — Copilot keeps the whole conversation visible. You'll know it worked when the updated plan reflects your change and nothing important has been deleted.

💬 Example: *"Move the 'print posters' task to Monday 9 March instead of the day before, and add a task to order 200 paper cups."*

## Step 5 — Save the plan somewhere you can use it
Once the plan looks right, you need to get it out of the chat. Look for the **copy icon** (two overlapping squares) under Copilot's reply — clicking it puts the whole plan on your clipboard so you can paste it anywhere. What happens after you click is a small "Copied" confirmation pops up briefly. Then open Word, Google Docs, Notes, Outlook or even a text message, right-click and choose **Paste**. If you'd rather not copy by hand, some versions of Copilot show a **Download** or **Export** button — look for an icon that looks like a downward arrow or three dots (⋯) near the reply. You'll know it worked when the plan appears in your chosen document, formatting and all.

💬 Example: Paste it into a new Word document and save it as *"Bake Sale Plan — March 14.docx"*.

## Step 6 — Share it with your team
Now send the plan to the people who'll actually do the work. Open your email (Outlook works beautifully with Copilot, but any email app is fine), start a new message, and paste the task list into the body. What you'll see after pasting is the list appears with its headings and bullet points intact. Address the email to your helpers, add a friendly one-liner at the top, and hit send. If some helpers prefer texting, you can paste the same list into a group chat instead — the formatting usually survives. You'll know it worked when everyone replies (even a 👍 emoji counts) and you have a rough sense of who's doing what by when.

💬 Example: *"Hi team, here's our plan for the 14 March bake sale — have a look and let me know if anything's missing. Thanks! Mia."*

## Common mistakes
- **Mistake:** Vague descriptions like *"plan my thing"*. **Fix:** Add the *what*, the *when* and the *who* — even rough versions. The more context you give, the less Copilot has to guess.
- **Mistake:** Treating the first answer as final. **Fix:** Plans almost always need 2–3 rounds of tweaks. Use the chat to adjust dates, swap owners or add tasks — that's what it's for.
- **Mistake:** Forgetting that Copilot can't book venues, send emails or reserve supplies for you. **Fix:** Use the plan as a *draft*, then do the real-world actions yourself or share the list with the person who can.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Planning a birthday dinner, a garage clean-up or a school fundraiser takes the same shape — a list, some owners, some dates. The 15-minute Copilot routine replaces the hour of staring at a blank page.
- **For your business or work:** Copilot is genuinely useful for kickoff meetings. Walk into the meeting with a first-draft plan already done, then spend the meeting adjusting it with your team instead of building it from zero.
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't worry about getting the prompt "right" on your first try. Treat the chat like a helpful colleague — describe your idea, see what comes back, and refine from there.

## Try it now
Open copilot.microsoft.com right now and type: *"Help me plan a half-day team offsite for 6 people next month. Budget $500. Give me a task list with owners and deadlines."* Watch what comes back, tweak one item, and you've just built your first AI-assisted plan in under two minutes.
